t: The Nok culture, named after the village in central Nigeria where its first sculpture was found in 1928, lasted from about 1500 BCE to around the turn of the Common Era.
From about 900 BCE its people made hollow clay figures of men and women with pierced eyes, elaborate hairstyles and jewellery, among the earliest sculpture known south of the Sahara.
Nok farmers grew pearl millet and smelted iron by the mid-first millennium BCE but lived in hamlets, not towns; looting for the art market has since ravaged most known sites.
dyk: The first Nok sculpture was found in 1928 about 7 metres down in a tin mine, and a head found in 1943 served for a year as a scarecrow in a yam field before Bernard Fagg recognised it.
ev: Farming communities settle in central Nigeria: the Early Nok phase begins
The Middle Nok phase opens; the first terracotta sculptures are made
Iron smelting begins in the Nok region, by current estimates (the dates are debated)
The Late Nok phase begins, known from only a few sites
Around the turn of the era the terracottas and the Nok settlements vanish from the record
Colonel Dent Young finds the first Nok terracotta in a tin mine near the village of Nok
A head used as a scarecrow leads Bernard Fagg to study the culture
Goethe University Frankfurt begins long-term excavations of Nok sites

f.homeland: Central Nigeria, in present-day southern Kaduna State and the neighbouring areas around the Jos Plateau; the village of Nok, which gave the culture its name, lies in southern Kaduna State
f.period: c. 1500 BCE to around the turn of the Common Era: Early Nok c. 1500–900 BCE, Middle Nok c. 900–300 BCE (the height of the terracottas and the first iron), Late Nok c. 300 BCE onwards
f.known: Hollow terracotta heads and figures with pierced eyes, elaborate hairstyles and jewellery; early iron smelting; pearl millet farming; small hamlets without towns
f.sources: Excavated sites such as Taruga, Samun Dukiya and Pangwari, above all the work of Goethe University Frankfurt since 2005; radiocarbon and thermoluminescence dates; plant remains and food residues in pots; no writing and no ancient accounts
